introduction.p: A sequence assigns a value to each integer index in its domain. Decimal approximations, Newton iterates, and successive integral approximations are examples. We will define convergence, prove criteria that establish a limit, and examine recursive sequences.

exercise.title: What does it mean for a sequence to converge?

statement.p: A sequence converges to L if its terms get arbitrarily close to L as n becomes large. In your own words, why is that stronger than saying the later terms look nearby in a table, and how is oscillating between two values different from growing without bound?

hint.p: Convergence requires every sufficiently late term to meet each prescribed tolerance. Persistent separated oscillations and unbounded growth prevent convergence, but oscillations of shrinking amplitude may converge.

exercise.title: Why can sampling a familiar formula fail to have a limit?

statement.p: The values a_n=\sin(n\pi/2) come from a continuous function, yet the sequence does not converge. In your own words, why is a sequence a list rather than a curve, and why can the sampled points refuse to settle even when the formula looks familiar?

hint.p: The index n jumps. What happens between integers is not part of the sequence, so a continuous picture can hide a jumping list.

exercise.title: Why do both monotonicity and boundedness matter?

statement.p: The Monotone Convergence Theorem says that an increasing sequence bounded above must converge, and likewise for a decreasing sequence bounded below. In your own words, why is monotone alone not enough, why is bounded alone not enough, and what completeness of the real line is doing in the argument?

hint.p: An increasing sequence with no ceiling grows without bound. Boundedness alone is not enough: a sequence alternating between two distinct values does not converge. Completeness supplies the least upper bound approached by an increasing bounded sequence.

subsection.title: The Cauchy criterion: convergence without knowing the limit
subsection.p: Sometimes an approximation has no known target value. We can still ask whether all sufficiently late terms are close to one another. A real sequence (a_n) is Cauchy if, for every \varepsilon>0, there is an integer N such that

statement.p: A sequence of real numbers converges to a real number if and only if it is Cauchy.

proof.p: If a_n\to L, choose N so that |a_n-L|<\varepsilon/2 for all n\ge N. The triangle inequality proves the Cauchy condition.
Conversely, a Cauchy sequence is bounded: take an eventual distance bound of 1 from one fixed term and then include the finitely many earlier terms. Define the tail bounds

Here \inf means greatest lower bound and \sup means least upper bound; completeness of the real line ensures both exist. The sequence \ell_N increases and u_N decreases, and both are bounded. The Monotone Convergence Theorem gives their limits. The Cauchy condition implies u_N-\ell_N\to0: if every pair of tail terms has distance less than \varepsilon, the tail's supremum minus its infimum is at most \varepsilon. Their limits are therefore the same number L. Since \ell_N\le a_N\le u_N, squeezing gives a_N\to L.

This tends to zero independently of m, so the sequence converges. We have proved existence of a limit before identifying it.

warning.title: Adjacent terms are not enough
warning.p: The condition |a_{n+1}-a_n|\to0 is weaker. For a_n=\ln n, adjacent differences \ln(1+1/n) tend to zero, but |a_{2n}-a_n|=\ln2. This sequence is not Cauchy.
The criterion depends on the number system being complete. Rational decimal truncations of \sqrt2 are Cauchy, yet they have no rational limit. They do have a real limit.

statement.p: Prove directly that a_n=1/n is Cauchy and that b_n=(-1)^n is not. Why does bounding just |a_{n+1}-a_n| fail to check the definition?

hint.p: For m,n\ge N, |1/m-1/n|\le1/N. Opposite-parity indices make the second distance equal to 2, however large the indices are. The definition requires every pair of late terms.

exercise.title: Why is a fixed-point equation not a proof of convergence?

statement.p: If a recursive sequence a_{n+1}=F(a_n) converges to L and F is continuous, then L=F(L). In your own words, why can that equation identify a possible limit without proving that the sequence actually converges?

hint.p: A possible landing place is not the same as landing. The recursion a_{n+1}=2-a_n has a fixed point at 1, but the sequence can bounce forever between two other values.

note.title: Moral
note.p: For a recursive sequence, the equation
can identify possible limits. It does not prove convergence. To prove convergence, we need more information, such as monotonicity and boundedness, or another argument that controls the iteration.

subsection.p: The next section uses sequences in a new way. Instead of studying a list of terms directly, we build a new sequence by adding the first n terms. If those partial sums settle toward a limit, we will call the result an infinite sum.
